title: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure
summary: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure is the parent technique for a family of actions that change the compute layer of a cloud account rather than reading it. The controlled API surface is the resource lifecycle itself: creating and terminating virtual machines, volumes and snapshots, reverting resources to earlier points in time, and adjusting the quotas, policies and regional settings that govern what can be deployed. The defensive problem is that every one of these calls is an authorised management action, so a signature or allow-list approach fails; what matters is the sequence and context. Typical adversary patterns include creating infrastructure to sidestep restrictive firewall rules or instance policies, mounting copies of data in a less monitored place, and then reverting or deleting resources so the running estate and its artefacts return to a clean state. Detection therefore lives in cloud audit telemetry, where resource creation and deletion events, identity, source address, user agent, and the volume of change are all recorded, and in the mismatch between those records and anything the workloads themselves still show. Defenders should baseline normal provisioning behaviour per role and alert on deletes that follow creates, on snapshot and volume operations outside change windows, and on configuration changes that widen what the account can deploy.

beginner.definition: Cloud computing means renting computers and storage over the internet instead of buying them. A cloud account holds virtual machines, disk volumes and copies called snapshots. This technique is about an attacker changing those rented pieces of infrastructure. They may add one, remove one, reset one, or change the account limits.
beginner.whyItMatters: These changes can erase evidence of an intrusion, such as logs stored on a machine that is then deleted. They can also create new machines that sit outside your normal security rules, giving the attacker a quiet place to work. Because every change uses valid credentials, it looks like normal administration. If nobody reviews the cloud activity records, the attacker can work for a long time without being noticed.
howItWorks: The attacker signs in to the cloud account with a stolen key or a hijacked session.
They list what exists and choose a target, such as a machine or a disk volume.
They create a new resource, for example a copy of a volume or a fresh machine.
They may loosen a setting, such as a firewall rule, or change an account limit.
They use the new resource to reach data or to run their own tools.
They delete or reset the resource so the account appears clean again.
beginner.example: Imagine a self storage facility. A person with a valid key rents a new unit, moves copies of their things into it, and works there quietly. The manager sees only that a unit was rented, not what happened inside. Later the renter empties the unit and leaves the keys, so nothing remains to look at.
takeaways: Cloud audit records are the main evidence for infrastructure changes.
Know what normal provisioning looks like so strange patterns stand out.
Limit which accounts may create or delete compute resources.

objectives: Describe which cloud components sit inside the compute infrastructure layer.
Explain why valid management actions still need monitoring and review.
Recognise patterns such as create then delete that suggest evasion.
Identify the cloud audit data that records these changes.
Outline access controls that reduce the impact of a stolen key.
